United States Magazine - 1956 Gravity Engines Are Coming  

 #UFOtwitter #ufo #uap 

It's, highly optimistic piece hyping the idea of anti-gravity propulsion (or "G-engines" for gravity engines) as the next big breakthrough in aviation and space travel.    

It's a sensational, highly optimistic piece hyping the idea of anti-gravity propulsion (or "G-engines" for gravity engines) as the next big breakthrough in aviation and space travel.  

Gravity is the most powerful energy source, far surpassing nuclear power. Engineers and companies (e.g., Glenn L. Martin Aircraft Co., Convair, Bell Aircraft, Lear Inc., Sperry Gyroscope) were supposedly researching ways to control or cancel gravity.  

This would enable fuel-less, weightless aircraft and spaceships capable of speeds up to 170,000 miles per second (close to the speed of light, ~186,000 mi/s).  

It ties into Einstein's relativity, the bending of light during solar eclipses, and early particle physics experiments (e.g., references to Dr. Stanley Deser, Dr. Richard Arnowitt, and gravity particles or "G-gravity" particles).  

Quotes from industry figures like Lawrence D. Bell ("We're already working with nuclear fuels and equipment to cancel out gravity") and others suggesting breakthroughs were imminent, potentially in the timeframe of the Manhattan Project.  

The illustration shows a futuristic cigar-shaped craft labeled EX-G1 with a pilot entering it, and a man gesturing toward a shadow implying gravity manipulation.   

Conclusion:   

As you can see for yourselves from article, they are talking about using electromagnetic propulsion to cancel the gravity to provide lift and propulsion for the vehicle, as well as using nuclear energy as an energy source – it's quite incredible to see something like this as early as 1956. 

This vehicle and Ivan Filimoneko vehicle he claims he created in 1957 are based on electromagnetic propulsion systems, which today we call it revolutionary. They are revolutionary, but they have existed since the 1950s.
